description: BeyondtheBlue is a team from Maputo, Mozambique, taking on the “Planet X and SPHEREx” challenge. The goal is to build a public-facing web tool that lets anyone explore SPHEREx sky images and see how they change over time, with features like a time slider, a blink comparator to spot moving objects, and a wavelength band selector. Let’s look beyond the blue, and find what moves in the dark.
summary:
BeyondtheBlue lets anyone watch the infrared sky change over time. A user types a star name or a pair of coordinates, and the tool finds every SPHEREx image of that spot, aligns them and plays them back as a short film. A star or brown dwarf that moved between visits jumps across the frame. Clicking any source returns its spectrum from 0.75 to 5 µm and its light curve, measured from every exposure that covers it.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared colours, far more than astronomers can check by eye. Volunteers comparing images found most of the brown dwarfs known today, and BeyondtheBlue brings that kind of search to SPHEREx with nothing to install and no gigabytes to download. The server reads only the pixels it needs from NASA’s archive, and the browser receives only small images, which matters for students on slow connections such as those common in Mozambique, where the project was developed.

The tool was tested on all five challenge targets. It measures Barnard’s Star moving 10.1″ per year (catalog: 10.39″) and recovers the 245-day cycle of R Draconis. New data releases appear automatically, and any view can be shared or embedded with a single link.
details:
What it does

BeyondtheBlue answers one question for anyone, not only astronomers: what changed in this patch of the infrared sky? You start with a single search box. It accepts an object name, RA/Dec in any common format, or even the coordinates pasted straight from the challenge text

The tool then finds every SPHEREx exposure covering that point, aligns them on a common north-up grid, and plays the epochs as a short movie. On the right, a spectrum built from more than 200 measurements across SPHEREx’s six detectors appears for the selected star

Tools to spot motion and variability

  • Blink and Difference modes subtract one epoch from another. In the difference image, a moving star becomes a red/blue pair, and the per-band light curve shows how its brightness changed.
  • Catalog overlays: Gaia DR3 and CatWISE sources with proper-motion arrows, plus a Sources table with the measured motion, flux and variability of every detected star. For Barnard’s Star we measure 10.07 ± 0.71″/yr.
  • Other surveys: unWISE images (3.4 and 4.6 µm) and Aladin Lite let users compare SPHEREx with WISE data taken more than a decade earlier.
  • Data quality: pixel flags (saturated, bad pixel, artefact) can be shown as a layer, and the Exposures tab lists every exposure used, so results are transparent and traceable.
  • Follow motion: the tool can shift and stack images along a proper motion, so even faint, fast movers stay centred. An “All frames” grid shows every epoch and band at once.
  • Light curves on the fly for every exposure, band by band, to study variable stars.
  • Display controls and “What changed”: speed, stretch, colour maps and smoothing. Each target gets a plain-language summary with its position now and in J2000, its proper motion, and the sources that changed in the field.

How it works

  1. Search: the server queries NASA/IPAC IRSA (SIA service) for all SPHEREx exposures of the field. The list of data collections (DR1, QR3) is read from IRSA itself, so new releases appear without code changes.
  2. Smart cutouts: each SPHEREx file is 60–70 MB. Using each detector’s known distortion, we predict the exact pixel rows needed with better than 0.1 px accuracy and download only those, in one HTTP request per file. This makes the tool fast enough for the public.
  3. Align and stack: images are reprojected to a common grid, sky-subtracted and grouped into epochs, with one image per band plus an all-detector stack for signal-to-noise.
  4. Detect: sources are matched between epochs, with astrometry at 0.01–0.02 px, to flag motion and variability automatically.
  5. Measure: aperture photometry on every exposure, following the proper motion, produces spectra and light curves.

Validated on all five challenge targets

  • Barnard’s Star: 10.1 ± 0.7″/yr toward 349° (catalog: 10.39″/yr toward 356°)
  • Epsilon Indi B: the brown-dwarf pair moves at 4.6″/yr together with its host star 7′ away (catalog: 4.68″/yr)
  • WISE 0855−0714: the challenge coordinates are from 2010. The tool warns that the object has moved 2.2′ and offers to follow it. Its spectrum shows the expected rise at 4–5 µm.
  • RW Aurigae: varies in all six bands and changes colour
  • R Draconis: its 245-day Mira cycle is recovered from 18 monthly blocks

Benefits and impact

Most known brown dwarfs and comets were found by volunteers comparing images. BeyondtheBlue brings that proven approach to SPHEREx, the first all-sky spectral survey, so the public can search for nearby cold objects, high-proper-motion stars and perhaps a distant Planet X. Because the tool reads 102 colours, users don’t just see that something moved: they can also see what it might be from its spectrum.

What makes it creative

  • It downloads only the pixels it needs, instead of gigabytes of files.
  • It combines a movie, a spectrum and a light curve for any source in a single click.
  • It warns automatically when the target’s coordinates are outdated.
  • Every view has a shareable URL and a ready-made embed code, so other projects can build on it.

Reliability

The five challenge targets are stored as snapshots, so they open in about 3 seconds even if the IRSA archive is down. Incomplete results are never cached. The code has 34 offline unit tests.

What makes it different

  • Spectra, not only blinking: WiseView, which inspired this project, blinks two WISE colours. BeyondtheBlue uses all 102 SPHEREx bands, so a moving source also comes with a spectrum that hints at what it is.
  • Partial reads instead of full downloads: this is what makes the tool fast enough for the public.
  • Measurements, not only pictures: motion and variability are measured automatically, with uncertainties, and compared against Gaia and CatWISE.
  • Warnings about outdated coordinates: the tool detects when coordinates are out of date for a fast-moving object, as with WISE 0855.
  • Follow-motion stacking: shifting and stacking along a proper motion brings out faint moving objects.

Potential

SPHEREx will keep mapping the sky every six months, so each new release adds an epoch and makes faint, slow movers easier to find. The planned next steps are:

  • a “flag a candidate” button that builds a review queue for volunteers;
  • alerts when new data arrives;
  • PSF fitting for fainter sources.

Because the pipeline relies only on standard archive services, the same approach could be extended to other surveys hosted by IRSA.

Known limitations

Measurements use quick-look aperture photometry, not PSF fitting. Motions below about 0.5″/yr are not yet detected, and automatic detection covers bright sources only.

Built with

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy and SciPy
  • Frontend: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Plotly for charts and Aladin Lite for sky maps
  • Quality and deployment: 34 offline unit tests, packaged with Docker
